How to Play 7 Wonders: Rules in the Order That Clicks

2026-09-28

How to play 7 Wonders: build the richest ancient civilization and outscore your neighbors after 3 ages of drafting cards. It plays 3 to 7 people in about 30 minutes, ages 10 and up. That is the whole promise. The hard part is that the turn order your brain expects simply does not exist.

I have taught this game to at least a dozen new players, and almost every one hits the same wall on the first round. There are no turns. Nobody is ever "not it." Everyone plays at the same time, so new players freeze, waiting for a signal that never comes. Here is the fix: 7 Wonders does not run on turns. It runs on a draft. Once you see that, the whole game unfolds in front of you.

The Goal, and the Card Draft at Its Core

Everyone starts with a wonder board, one of the seven ancient wonders, and three coins. Your goal is the most victory points after three ages of play. Each age, you build your city out of cards, and 18 cards total end up in front of you across the whole game, 6 per age.

Every age, each player is dealt 7 cards. You look at them, secretly pick the one you want to keep, and pass the rest to your neighbor. In Ages I and III you pass the hand left; in Age II you pass it right instead, so the direction flips every round of that age. It is one detail, and the Age card backs show the arrow, but it is the one rule first timers keep getting wrong.

The Move You Make Every Round: Pick, Play, Pass

Each round has three beats, and they happen for everyone at the same time. First, everyone secretly picks one card. Then everyone reveals at once. Then you decide what to do with it, and pass the leftover pile.

You have three options with the card you kept. Build the building on it, if you can pay. Spend it as the next stage of your wonder. Or sell it facedown for 3 coins. The last card left in every hand, on the final round of an age, is simply discarded. Nobody gets it.

Here is the key insight for a new player. Because the hand keeps passing, the cards come back to you from the other side two rounds later. A card you skip this round is a card you might see again. That is what makes the draft feel clever instead of random. You are not just drawing. You are steering a river of cards that flows around the table.

The Money and Resource Math

Some cards are free. Some cost coins, and you start with only 3, so coin cards are a real decision, not a convenience. Most early buildings cost resources. Brown cards make raw materials like wood and ore, grey cards make finished goods like glass and paper. You pay costs from the production your city already has.

Pay attention to this number: 2 coins for every resource you borrow. If you cannot produce enough on your own, you can buy from either neighbor at a fixed 2 coins per resource. No haggling. Unlike Catan, the price never changes and you never need their permission. But there is a catch: you can only borrow from brown and grey cards, never from yellow commercial ones. The yellow cards in your neighbor's city are off limits to you.

Then there are chains. Some cards carry a symbol that links to another card, and if you already own that linked building, the next one is free. This is where combos live. A smart chain built over two ages quietly saves you the fortune everyone else is spending.

The Wonder Board: Your Built-In Plan

Your wonder board is a mini game of its own. Each one can be built in stages, left to right, and each stage you complete gives you a permanent perk. One stage hands you 3 coins. Another gives you a free extra resource every round. The later stages are usually worth victory points outright.

To build a stage, you feed it a card from your hand, facedown, and check the wonder's own cost in resources first. You never have to build your wonder. It is a fallback, a place to park cards that are not useful on their own, and that makes it the most forgiving part of the game for beginners. Stuck with a card you cannot pay for and do not want? Sell it for coins, or tuck it under your wonder.

Then Comes the Fighting

At the end of every age, your cities compare military strength. Count the shields on your red military cards and compare them to the neighbor on your left and the neighbor on your right. Beat one of them and you grab a victory token worth 1 point in Age I, 3 points in Age II, and 5 in Age III. Lose to both of your neighbors and you take a defeat token worth minus 1.

Nobody is eliminated. There is no knockout. It is just a points swing, but a big one. A single red card bought in Age II can flip a 3 point token your way, and in the final age a military win is worth 5 points, more than almost any building you could draw. Ignore the red cards only if you are sure you can win elsewhere.

Here is the part nobody tells you: the cards are the game, not your city. Because the hands pass around the table, every card you build is a card your neighbor now cannot have. The best 7 Wonders players take cards they do not need, purely to block the person to their left. I lost my first four games before a friend pointed this out, then won the next one with a worse hand than any of my losses. Nothing about my city changed. Only who I was blocking. Drafting is a quiet war of denial dressed up as a peaceful building game, and that hidden war is why the game never gets boring.

The Scoring That Trips Up Every First Game

When the third age ends, you score seven things: your wonder stages, your coins at 3 coins to 1 point, your military tokens (which can be negative), your blue civilian card points, your yellow commercial points, your green science, and your purple guild cards. The whole tally takes a few minutes and the score pad walks you through it in order.

The science cards are the confusing one, so let me kill the confusion now. Each science card shows one of three symbols: a tablet, a gear, or a wheel. Identical symbols score the square of how many you have, so 3 of the same symbol score 9, and a full set of all three different symbols scores 7 more. A city with 3 gears, 2 tablets, and 1 wheel scores 9 for gears, 4 for tablets, 1 for the lone wheel, plus 7 for one complete set, for 21 points in one scoring line. Science does not look scary on the table. It quietly wins whole games if you commit to it.

What to Buy, and What to Skip

So now you know how to play. The real question is which box reaches the table on your next game night.

The base 7 Wonders (New Edition) handles 3 to 7 players and runs about 30 minutes. It is the version everyone means, with the full details on my 7 Wonders page. Note the floor of 3 players. It is a game night game, not a date night game. If you mostly have two people at the table, get 7 Wonders Duel instead, which I ranked on my best 2-player games list. The full game and Duel are different enough that you can own both, and plenty of people do.

If the base game grabs you, the Leaders expansion adds a fourth quick draft of special leaders before the game even starts, and Cities adds a second hand every round with a third age of black city cards. Both are excellent, but skip them until the base game feels solved. That took me twenty plays.

And if drafting itself sounds like too much, Sushi Go! is the same passing mechanic in a 15 minute, under $12 shell. It is a perfect way to learn whether your group likes drafting before you commit to the big box.

The Honest Truth About 7 Wonders

The first game is slow. The symbols are the whole interface of this game, and they take one full play to learn. You will stare at a card, trying to figure out what a brown circle means, while the military conflict fires and the hand rushes past you. Everyone has this first game. It is the price of admission.

But here is the other side. The second game is under 30 minutes, smooth, and you start spotting combos you missed. That is why the standard advice for this game is so stubborn: give it two plays before you judge it. The first game teaches you the alphabet. The second game is where you actually read.

Here is the Shelf Test. Would this game survive 10 plays on your shelf? Yes, and far more. It is the rare drafting game with zero downtime, so it is the one I pull out when the table count is an awkward 5 or 6 and nobody wants to wait through long turns. The New Edition lists at $59.99 and bounces between about $45 and $55 on Amazon; GameNerdz had it at $47.99 when I last checked. Under $50 is a fair deal. Above $52, wait a week, it comes back down. Grab the box, run the draft above, and may the person to your left never forgive you.
